namespace.why: This repository already holds at least eight incompatible curriculum naming schemes and the last thing it needs is a ninth. Two surfaces built concurrently already spell the M1 Codex cards this way: `codexCardIds` in packages/curriculum/src/conceptRegistry.ts, and `codexCardIds` on every card of the module deck in apps/web/src/module/m1Module.ts. Both took the spelling from Mission-Slate §4.9. This file adopts it unchanged and supplies the one thing neither of them has — what each card actually says.
namespace.structuralNote: The mission segment `MD01` is inherited from §4.9 and is a known wart. packages/curriculum/src/types.ts deliberately dropped the mission segment from CONCEPT ids because a spiral concept cannot belong to mission day one, and the same argument applies to a card: CONSENT_GROUND recurs under 8.15(E) and 8.19(A) later in the chapter. Renaming the cards to `BOS.CARD.*` is the right end state and is a three-file change (this file, the concept registry, the module deck). It is not done here because a rename that lands in one of three files is worse than the wart.
namespace.conceptIdsUsed: Canonical, from packages/curriculum. Each card carries the legacy learner id too, so a consumer that has not adopted the registry yet still resolves.

lifecycle.learnedAt: Set when the student completes the module that sources the card. Every card below is sourced by exactly one module card, so 'learned' is a fact about the deck rather than a judgement about the student.
lifecycle.pvpLegalAt: Minted only at 100% mastery of the card's concept on the chapter capstone. No duel result and no mission clear may set it. A student can hold all nine of these cards as learned, clear M1 on the first attempt, and still have none of them PvP-legal.
lifecycle.whatTheCodexIsFor: Mission-Slate §1.7: the Codex is the index of what a player can be asked. Facing a question whose card you do not hold means you probably miss it, fight that round on the wrong-answer grant, and go learn it. Cards are never played as a deck.
lifecycle.mintedByThisMission: Nothing. §4.10 is explicit that M1 mints no cards and that duel performance is evidence rather than a granting event.

cards.title: The debt the war left
cards.proposition: The war with France ended in 1763 and left Britain owing more money than it ever had, with an army in America still to pay for. This card is the money problem itself — the hole the war dug. It does not say who Parliament decided should fill it, and it is not the order the events came in.
cards.note: Three names, one war. Every rubric that touches this card treats them as identical, which is the correct-but-unusually-worded case §1.7 requires the evaluation set to cover.

cards.title: Who Parliament made pay
cards.proposition: Faced with that debt, Parliament decided the colonies — not taxpayers at home — should supply part of the money. This card is the choice of payer, and only that: who Parliament picked. It does not describe the debt that forced the choice, and it does not settle which came first.

cards.title: Which came first
cards.proposition: The order runs one way and only one way: the debt came first, and the tax is Parliament's answer to it, never its cause. This card is the sequence — debt, then policy, then stamp. It is not the size of the debt and not the choice of who pays; it is the claim about what followed what.
cards.note: The only card that spans all three concepts in what it asserts, which is why the synthesis card is its source rather than any one concept card.

cards.title: What the stamp taxes
cards.proposition: The Act taxes printed and official paper — newspapers, handbills, deeds, court papers, licences, playing cards — and nothing else. A bolt of cloth off a ship and a private handwritten letter fall outside it. This card is the boundary of what is taxed: not when the tax starts, and not whose trade it strikes hardest.
cards.note: The exemplars are part of the proposition rather than illustration. Five of the six stamp-scope items turn on a boundary, and a boundary with no instances on either side of it is not teachable in forty seconds.

cards.title: When it starts
cards.proposition: The Act passed in March 1765, but the duty is not owed until 1 November — so through the summer the law exists while the tax has not yet begun, which is why the town is still free to argue it. This card is only the timing: the gap between a law passed and a tax coming due.

cards.title: Who it hits hardest
cards.proposition: A printer's whole trade is printed paper, so the one thing the Act taxes is the one thing the shop sells — which is why it lands harder on a printing house than on a cooper or a ropemaker. This card is who the tax burdens most, not the list of what counts as taxable paper.

cards.title: No vote in Parliament
cards.proposition: Boston elects its own town meeting and its own members of the Massachusetts assembly, but it elects no member of the Parliament that laid this tax. This card is the plain fact of who Boston does and does not choose. It is not the principle that makes the fact matter, and not the reply to London's defence.

cards.title: Only the chosen may tax
cards.proposition: A tax is legitimate only when it is laid by a body the taxed people chose; the objection is to who laid it, not to what it costs — Boston would say the same if the stamp cost a farthing. This card is the principle. It is not the bare fact of Boston's missing vote, and not the answer to the claim that Parliament already speaks for everyone.
cards.note: The most load-bearing card in the mission and the one most often half-held: students reliably reach the objection and land it on the price.

cards.title: Lawful is not consent
cards.proposition: London's defence is that Parliament already speaks for every subject, voted for or not — 'virtual representation.' Boston's reply: a lawful vote taken by men the town never chose is still not the town's consent. This card is the answer to that one claim. It is not the general principle, and not the bare fact of the missing vote.
cards.whyNew: Mission-Slate §4.9 authored SPEAKS_FOR_ALL and LAWFUL_BUT_UNJUST against eight cards, none of which carried the claim either item answers. Two items in the bank therefore rested on a proposition the module never taught, which §4.7 itself says must be fixed on one side or the other. It is fixed here, on the module side, and this card is that proposition. It is the ninth card, and the concept registry's REPRESENTATION entry lists only two — that entry needs this id appended.
